questions.scenario: Your wallet API accepts any token signed by the bank's Keycloak realm. A tester takes a valid token issued for the bank's internal HR API and calls your transfer endpoint with it, and it works.
questions.question: Which validation is missing?
options: Signature validation
TLS on the endpoint
Expiry validation
Audience (aud) validation, so only tokens intended for the wallet API are accepted
questions.explanation: The token is genuine and unexpired, but it was issued for a different API. Checking that aud includes your API prevents tokens meant for one service being replayed against another.

questions.scenario: A developer says JWT payloads are safe for storing the customer's BVN because 'the token is signed'.
questions.question: Why is this wrong?
options: Signatures expire after 15 minutes
A signature proves who created the token and that it was not changed; it does not hide the contents, which anyone holding the token can decode
BVNs are not personal data
JWTs are encrypted by default, so it is fine
questions.explanation: A signed JWT (JWS) is only Base64URL-encoded. Sensitive data must not be placed in claims unless you use encrypted JWTs (JWE), and even then it is usually better to keep it server-side.

questions.scenario: A mobile banking app needs to call your API on behalf of a signed-in customer.
questions.question: Which OAuth 2.0 flow should it use?
options: Resource owner password credentials
Authorization code with PKCE
Implicit
Client credentials
questions.explanation: Authorization code with PKCE is the recommended flow for user-facing public clients. Client credentials has no user; the password and implicit grants are deprecated.

questions.scenario: A nightly reconciliation job (no user involved) must call the ledger API.
questions.question: Which grant fits?
options: No authentication, because it runs inside the network
Authorization code with PKCE using an operations staff member's login
Client credentials, with the job authenticating as its own client and receiving only the scopes it needs
Sharing an admin user's password with the job
questions.explanation: Machine-to-machine calls use client credentials. Borrowing a person's identity breaks audit trails, and network location is not authentication.

questions.scenario: Your service rotates refresh tokens. An attacker steals a refresh token and uses it first; later the real user's app presents the same (already used) token.
questions.question: What should the service do?
options: Treat it as theft: revoke the whole token family and require a new login
Issue a new token pair to whoever presents it
Extend the token's expiry
Ignore the second request
questions.explanation: Reuse of a rotated refresh token means two parties hold it. Revoking the family cuts off the attacker, at the cost of asking the user to sign in again.

questions.scenario: You are listing the checks a resource server must perform on every JWT.
questions.question: Which of these are required? (Choose two.)
options: The token's sub claim is an email address
The token is longer than 500 characters
The token has not expired (exp) and comes from the expected issuer (iss)
The signature verifies with the issuer's key, using an expected algorithm
questions.explanation: Signature with an allowed algorithm, issuer and time-based claims (plus audience) are the core checks. Token length and the format of sub are not security properties.

questions.scenario: A back-office web application signs staff in with oauth2Login and keeps their tokens in the server-side HTTP session.
questions.question: Should CSRF protection be disabled for this application?
options: Yes: all Spring applications should disable CSRF
Yes: OAuth2 makes CSRF impossible
No: it authenticates with a session cookie that browsers attach automatically, so CSRF protection must stay on
It does not matter for internal staff
questions.explanation: oauth2Login results in a cookie-based session, which is exactly what CSRF attacks exploit. Only bearer-token APIs without cookies can safely disable it.
